Chapter Eight: The Challenge of Self-Interest
You know, we all like to think we’re standing up for what’s right. But here’s a tough reality—when real change starts to threaten our own comfort, or maybe our sense of security, self-interest often sneaks in and gets in the way. And honestly, that can be hard to admit.
Picture this: a homeowner hears about plans for new affordable housing in their neighborhood. On paper, it sounds great. But then, that little voice starts whispering... What if property values drop? What if the neighborhood changes in ways I’m not ready for? Suddenly, the idea doesn’t seem so simple. The urge to say no—even if it means others miss out on opportunities—can feel overwhelming.
Most of us don’t want to think of ourselves as selfish. We want to help, just... not if it costs us too much. And this is where antiracism work gets deeply personal. It asks us to look, honestly, at where our own interests might be holding us back—and to be willing to make sacrifices, sometimes, for the greater good.
People who’ve really wrestled with these questions have discovered something important: real change takes more than just good intentions or empathy. It means being willing to give up some privilege. To share what we have. To support policies that might not, honestly, benefit us directly.
It’s not easy. It’s about facing our own fears and insecurities, and choosing to stand with others—even when it feels risky. It’s about picking solidarity over self-protection.
And this challenge? It isn’t limited to one group or community. You’ll find it everywhere—in every neighborhood, every workplace, every institution. The real work of antiracism is recognizing those moments when self-interest creeps in, and choosing justice, even when it feels tough.
But here’s some hope: over time, making these choices starts to reshape communities. People begin to feel a sense of shared purpose. We start to believe—deep down—that everyone’s well-being is connected. The road ahead can seem uncertain, and yeah, the risks are real.
But think about the reward: a society that’s more just, more equitable, and more connected. That’s worth every bit of effort.
